quote: Kennt die Gartenfrau besser, was eine Ebene ist, weil sie sicherer planiren kann oder was eine Gerade ist, weil sie die Wege auf dem Gemüsebeet exakt[?] abstecken kann oder was stetig gekrümmt ist, weil sie die geschwungenen Weglinien sicherer macht?
english: Does the garden woman know better what a plane is because she can level more surely, or what a straight line is because she can stake out the paths on the vegetable bed exactly, or what is continuously curved because she makes the curved path lines more surely?
topic: Loose reflections: a soldier's respect for a commander who shoots well, the inessential nature of words compared with the thought as 'invariant', whether practical activities such as gardening give better knowledge of geometric concepts, how interests in the same object differ, and whether geometric drawing trains geometric intuition.

triage.modern_statement: This is not a mathematical research question. It is a philosophical and educational question about where geometric concepts come from. Hilbert asks whether practical skill (levelling ground, staking out straight paths, laying out smooth curved paths) gives someone a better grasp of the concepts of plane, straight line and continuous curvature. Put in modern terms, it asks whether hands-on or empirical skill helps with conceptual understanding of geometric primitives, compared with understanding them through axioms. That is a question for the philosophy and teaching of geometry. It cannot be posed as a theorem or a conjecture.
triage.answered_by: No one. There is nothing mathematical here to answer. The note fits Hilbert's broader thinking about intuition and axioms in geometry, which he worked out in his geometry lectures of 1891–1902 and in the Grundlagen der Geometrie of 1899. In the Grundlagen, points, lines and planes are taken as undefined 'systems of things' described only by the axioms. That treatment suggests skill at practical construction is beside the point for the formal concept. However, I found no source that discusses this particular notebook entry.

evidence.claim: In the Grundlagen der Geometrie, Hilbert takes three systems of things (points, lines, planes) and basic relations as undefined, characterised only by axioms. They are not defined by intuition or practical construction.

Hilbert's lecture notes on the foundations of geometry from 1891–1902 have been published, edited by Hallett and Majer (Springer, 2004). They are the published record of his views on intuition and the axiomatic method.

Hilbert's mathematical notebooks (Cod. Ms. D. Hilbert 600) are held in his Nachlass at SUB Göttingen. A notebook entry has been identified as a known problem in at least one case, the 24th problem. Nothing similar has been reported for this entry.
Hilbert's interest in geometric intuition later produced the book Anschauliche Geometrie, written with Cohn-Vossen.

triage.why: The note is a rhetorical, epistemological reflection. It belongs with the other loose remarks on the same page: words as inessential compared with the thought as 'invariant', and whether drawing trains geometric intuition. It contains no mathematical statement that could be proved or refuted. It is not among the 23 problems or the 24th problem. Related themes, such as how practical activity relates to geometric concepts and the role of intuition, are still discussed in the philosophy and teaching of mathematics. Since there is no research problem here, whether it is 'active' can't really be decided. My searches found no secondary literature that discusses this specific entry.
